metadata.title: Double Descent Demystified: Identifying, Interpreting & Ablating the Sources of a Deep Learning Puzzle
metadata.authors: Schaeffer, Khona, Robertson, Boopathy, Pistunova, Rocks, Fiete, Koyejo

nodes.name: Supervised regression dataset
nodes.section: 2 Notation and Terminology
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{D} \defeq \{(\vec{x}_n, y_n)\}_{n=1}^N$ with covariates $\vec{x}_n \in \mathbb{R}^D$ and targets $y_n \in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Training set of N covariate-target pairs in dimension D.

nodes.name: Design matrix and target vector
nodes.section: 2 Notation and Terminology
nodes.statement: $X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}$ stacks the covariates $\vec{x}_n$ as rows and $Y \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 1}$ stacks the targets $y_n$.

nodes.name: Linear regression model
nodes.section: 2 Notation and Terminology
nodes.statement: A linear model assumes $f(\vec{x}) = \vec{x} \cdot \vec{\beta}$, with parameters $\hat{\vec{\beta}} \in \mathbb{R}^D$ chosen so that $\vec{x} \cdot \vec{\beta} \approx y$.

nodes.name: Overparameterized / underparameterized / interpolation threshold
nodes.section: 2 Notation and Terminology
nodes.statement: A model is overparameterized (underconstrained) if $N < P$ and underparameterized (overconstrained) if $N > P$; the interpolation threshold is $N = P$, where the model can perfectly interpolate the training points.
nodes.statement_clean: Three regimes based on ratio of parameters P to data N.

nodes.name: Polynomial feature map
nodes.section: 3 Visual Intuition from Polynomial Regression
nodes.statement: $\vec{\phi}_P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^P$ maps $x \mapsto (\phi_1(x), \ldots, \phi_P(x))^T$ where $\phi_i$ are polynomials (Legendre polynomials in the simulations).
nodes.statement_clean: Feature lift to a P-dimensional polynomial basis.

nodes.name: Gram matrix and second-moment matrix
nodes.section: 4 Mathematical Intuition from Ordinary Linear Regression
nodes.statement: Gram matrix $X X^T \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}$ (outer product matrix) and second-moment matrix $X^T X \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}$ derived from $X$.
nodes.statement_clean: Two derived matrices used in linear regression solutions.

nodes.name: Singular value decomposition of $X$
nodes.section: 4 Mathematical Intuition from Ordinary Linear Regression
nodes.statement: $X = U \Sigma V^T$ with $U, V$ orthonormal and $\Sigma$ diagonal; equivalently $X = \sum_{r=1}^{\mathrm{rank}(X)} \sigma_r \vec{u}_r \vec{v}_r^T$ with singular values $\sigma_1 > \cdots > \sigma_R > 0$.
nodes.statement_clean: SVD of the training feature matrix.

nodes.name: Ideal linear parameters and residual errors
nodes.section: 4 Mathematical Intuition from Ordinary Linear Regression
nodes.statement: There exist (unknown) ideal parameters $\vec{\beta}^* \in \mathbb{R}^D$ and residuals $E \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 1}$ such that $Y = X \vec{\beta}^* + E$; residuals may be noise or deterministic structure not capturable by the model class.
nodes.statement_clean: Notation separating signal X beta* from model-class-residuals E.

nodes.name: Underparameterized least-squares problem
nodes.section: 4 Mathematical Intuition from Ordinary Linear Regression
nodes.statement: $\hat{\vec{\beta}}_{under} \defeq \arg\min_{\vec{\beta}} \frac{1}{N} \sum_n \|\vec{x}_n \cdot \vec{\beta} - y_n\|_2^2 = \arg\min_{\vec{\beta}} \|X \vec{\beta} - Y\|_F^2$.
nodes.statement_clean: Classical OLS optimization in the underparameterized regime.

nodes.name: Overparameterized minimum-norm interpolation problem
nodes.section: 4 Mathematical Intuition from Ordinary Linear Regression
nodes.statement: $\hat{\vec{\beta}}_{over} \defeq \arg\min_{\vec{\beta}} \|\vec{\beta}\|_2^2$ subject to $\vec{x}_n \cdot \vec{\beta} = y_n$ for all $n$; the smallest-norm interpolant of the training data.
nodes.statement_clean: Min-norm interpolation chosen because it is what gradient descent implicitly minimizes.

nodes.name: Closed-form OLS estimator (underparameterized)
nodes.section: 4 Mathematical Intuition from Ordinary Linear Regression
nodes.statement: The solution of the underparameterized least-squares problem is $\hat{\vec{\beta}}_{under} = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T Y$.
assumptions: $X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}$ with $N > D$ so that $X^T X$ is invertible

nodes.name: Min-norm interpolant via Gram matrix (overparameterized)
nodes.section: 4 Mathematical Intuition from Ordinary Linear Regression
nodes.statement: The solution of the overparameterized min-norm interpolation problem is $\hat{\vec{\beta}}_{over} = X^T (X X^T)^{-1} Y$, where $X X^T$ is invertible because it is full rank in the overparameterized regime.
assumptions: $X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}$ with $N < D$ so that $X X^T$ is full rank

nodes.name: Lagrangian derivation of $\hat{\vec{\beta}}_{over}$
nodes.section: 4 Mathematical Intuition from Ordinary Linear Regression
nodes.statement: Form the Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}(\vec{\beta}, \vec{\lambda}) = \|\vec{\beta}\|_2^2 + \vec{\lambda}^T (Y - X \vec{\beta})$ and set its gradients to zero to recover $\hat{\vec{\beta}}_{over} = X^T (X X^T)^{-1} Y$.

nodes.name: Form Lagrangian
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{L}(\vec{\beta}, \vec{\lambda}) \defeq \|\vec{\beta}\|_2^2 + \vec{\lambda}^T (Y - X \vec{\beta})$ with multipliers $\vec{\lambda} \in \mathbb{R}^N$.

nodes.name: Stationarity in $\vec{\beta}$
nodes.statement: $\nabla_{\vec{\beta}} \mathcal{L} = 2 \hat{\vec{\beta}} - X^T \vec{\lambda} = 0 \Rightarrow \hat{\vec{\beta}}_{over} = \tfrac{1}{2} X^T \vec{\lambda}$.

nodes.name: Primal feasibility yields $\vec{\lambda}$
nodes.statement: $\nabla_{\vec{\lambda}} \mathcal{L} = 0 \Rightarrow Y = \tfrac{1}{2} X X^T \vec{\lambda} \Rightarrow \vec{\lambda} = 2 (X X^T)^{-1} Y$.

nodes.name: Substitute to obtain $\hat{\vec{\beta}}_{over}$
nodes.statement: Substituting $\vec{\lambda}$ into the expression for $\hat{\vec{\beta}}$ gives $\hat{\vec{\beta}}_{over} = X^T (X X^T)^{-1} Y$.

nodes.name: Predictions of fitted models
nodes.section: 4 Mathematical Intuition from Ordinary Linear Regression
nodes.statement: $\hat{y}_{test,under} = \vec{x}_{test} \cdot (X^T X)^{-1} X^T Y$ and $\hat{y}_{test,over} = \vec{x}_{test} \cdot X^T (X X^T)^{-1} Y$.

nodes.name: Spectral decomposition of prediction error (variance term)
nodes.section: 4 Mathematical Intuition from Ordinary Linear Regression
nodes.statement: Writing $X = U \Sigma V^T$ and $Y = X \vec{\beta}^* + E$, the prediction-error variance term satisfies $\hat{y}_{test,under} - y_{test}^* = \sum_{r=1}^R \frac{1}{\sigma_r} (\vec{x}_{test} \cdot \vec{v}_r)(\vec{u}_r \cdot E)$ in the underparameterized regime.

nodes.name: Overparameterized prediction-error decomposition (bias + variance)
nodes.section: 4 Mathematical Intuition from Ordinary Linear Regression
nodes.statement: $\hat{y}_{test,over} - y_{test}^* = \vec{x}_{test} \cdot (X^T (X X^T)^{-1} X - I_D) \vec{\beta}^* + \sum_{r=1}^R \frac{1}{\sigma_r} (\vec{x}_{test} \cdot \vec{v}_r)(\vec{u}_r \cdot E)$, splitting into a bias term and the same variance term.
conclusions: bias-variance split with explicit closed form for both terms

nodes.name: Derivation of error decomposition via SVD substitution
nodes.section: 4 Mathematical Intuition from Ordinary Linear Regression
nodes.statement: Substitute $Y = X \vec{\beta}^* + E$ into the prediction formulas, simplify $\vec{x}_{test} \cdot (X^T X)^{-1} X^T X \vec{\beta}^* = \vec{x}_{test} \cdot \vec{\beta}^*$, and replace the remaining $X$ with its SVD to obtain the singular-mode sum.

nodes.name: Substitute $Y = X \vec{\beta}^* + E$
nodes.statement: $\hat{y}_{test,under} = \vec{x}_{test} \cdot (X^T X)^{-1} X^T (X \vec{\beta}^* + E)$.

nodes.name: Cancel $(X^T X)^{-1} X^T X = I$
nodes.statement: Yields $\hat{y}_{test,under} = \vec{x}_{test} \cdot \vec{\beta}^* + \vec{x}_{test} \cdot (X^T X)^{-1} X^T E$, so $\hat{y}_{test,under} - y_{test}^* = \vec{x}_{test} \cdot (X^T X)^{-1} X^T E$.

nodes.name: Replace $X$ with $U \Sigma V^T$
nodes.statement: $(X^T X)^{-1} X^T = V \Sigma^{+} U^T$ gives $\sum_{r=1}^R \frac{1}{\sigma_r}(\vec{x}_{test}\cdot\vec{v}_r)(\vec{u}_r \cdot E)$.

nodes.name: Three factors that together create double descent
nodes.section: 4 Mathematical Intuition from Ordinary Linear Regression
nodes.statement: Double descent arises when three quantities simultaneously grow extreme: (i) some $1/\sigma_r$ is large (a small-but-nonzero singular value of $X$), (ii) $\vec{u}_r \cdot E$ is large (training residuals project onto that mode), and (iii) $\vec{x}_{test} \cdot \vec{v}_r$ is large (test point varies along that mode).
assumptions: the variance-term decomposition of TP459.3 / TP459.4 holds
conclusions: the per-mode contribution $\frac{1}{\sigma_r}(\vec{x}_{test}\cdot\vec{v}_r)(\vec{u}_r \cdot E)$ explodes only when all three factors are simultaneously extreme

nodes.name: Smallest non-zero singular value is minimized at the interpolation threshold
nodes.section: 4 Mathematical Intuition from Ordinary Linear Regression
nodes.statement: As one approaches $N = P = D$, the smallest non-zero singular value of $X$ is probabilistically driven to its lowest value, because each new training datum is unlikely to add substantial variance in a fresh orthogonal direction; this can be made rigorous via the Marchenko-Pastur distribution.
assumptions: random training features $X$ with finite second moments
conclusions: $\min_r \sigma_r$ attains its smallest typical value near $N = P = D$

nodes.name: Necessary conditions: removing any factor kills double descent
nodes.section: 5 When Does Double Descent Not Occur?
nodes.statement: Double descent does not occur if any of the three factors is absent: (a) no small-but-nonzero singular values of $X$ (e.g. ridge regression); (b) $\vec{x}_{test}$ lies in the leading-singular-direction subspace of $X$; or (c) the best model in the class has zero residual $E$ on the training data.
conclusions: absence of any single factor suffices to prevent the test-error spike at the interpolation threshold

nodes.name: Polynomial regression sweep
nodes.section: 3 Visual Intuition from Polynomial Regression
nodes.statement: Fit a linear-in-$\vec{\beta}_P$ model $y \approx \vec{\phi}_P(x) \cdot \vec{\beta}_P$ to data generated from $y(x) = 2x + \cos(25 x)$, sweeping $P$ from $1$ to $200$ to visualize bias and variance across regimes.
input: Data $(x_n, y_n)$ with $y(x) = 2 x + \cos(25 x)$ and $x \in [-1,1]$
output: Test error curve as a function of $P$ exhibiting double descent

nodes.name: Ordinary linear regression with sweep over $N$
nodes.section: 5 Empirical Evidence on Real Data with Linear Regression
nodes.statement: Run ordinary linear regression on a tabular dataset (WHO Life Expectancy, California Housing, or Diabetes), sweeping the number of training data $N$ and using the underparameterized OLS estimator or the overparameterized min-norm estimator according to whether $N > D$ or $N < D$.
input: Tabular dataset with features in $\mathbb{R}^D$ and scalar target
output: Test mean-squared-error curve as a function of $N$
Smallest non-zero singular value of $X$ as a function of $N$

nodes.name: Three-factor ablation procedure for double descent
nodes.section: 5 When Does Double Descent Not Occur?
nodes.statement: Causally test the three-factor hypothesis by, while sweeping $N$, separately (1) cutting off small singular values of $X$, (2) projecting $\vec{x}_{test}$ onto the training-feature subspace, and (3) replacing $Y$ by $X \vec{\beta}^*$ so that residuals vanish.
input: Choice of which factor to ablate
output: Test-error curves with and without the ablation, showing the spike disappears when any of the three factors is removed

nodes.name: Singular-value cutoff ablation
nodes.statement: Compute the SVD $X = U \Sigma V^T$ and zero out all singular values below a chosen cutoff before forming $\hat{\vec{\beta}}$.

nodes.name: Project test features onto training subspace
nodes.statement: Replace $\vec{x}_{test}$ by its projection onto the column span of $V$ (equivalently the leading singular modes of $X$) before computing $\hat{y}_{test}$.

nodes.name: Linearize the targets
nodes.statement: Fit $\vec{\beta}^*$ on the full dataset, then replace $Y$ by $X \vec{\beta}^*$ and $y_{test}^*$ by $\vec{x}_{test} \cdot \vec{\beta}^*$ so that $E \equiv 0$.

nodes.name: Polynomial regression of $y = 2x + \cos(25 x)$
nodes.section: 3 Visual Intuition from Polynomial Regression
nodes.statement: Concrete one-dimensional example with target $y(x) = 2 x + \cos(25 x)$ on $x \in [-1,1]$ used to visualize the bias-variance trade-off and double descent as $P$ varies.

nodes.name: Linear regression on WHO Life Expectancy
nodes.section: 5 Empirical Evidence on Real Data with Linear Regression
nodes.statement: Ordinary linear regression on the WHO Life Expectancy dataset shows a sharp test-error spike at the interpolation threshold; the smallest non-zero singular value of $X$ also bottoms out there.

nodes.name: Linear regression on California Housing
nodes.section: 5 Empirical Evidence on Real Data with Linear Regression
nodes.statement: Ordinary linear regression on the California Housing dataset reproduces double descent with a corresponding minimum of $\min_r \sigma_r(X)$ at $N = P$.

nodes.name: Linear regression on Diabetes
nodes.section: 5 Empirical Evidence on Real Data with Linear Regression
nodes.statement: Ordinary linear regression on the Diabetes dataset (sklearn) again exhibits double descent and the singular-value dip at the interpolation threshold.

nodes.name: Student-teacher synthetic ablation
nodes.section: 5 When Does Double Descent Not Occur?
nodes.statement: Synthetic student-teacher dataset on which the three ablations of AP459.3 each remove the test-error spike; serves as a controlled illustration of ClP459.3.

nodes.name: Shallow nonlinear autoencoders (Henighan et al. 2023)
nodes.section: 6 Intuition Extends to Nonlinear Models
nodes.statement: Shallow nonlinear autoencoders display double descent between a 'data-point feature' and 'generalizing feature' regime; the tutorial's three-factor view explains this as the same Gram-vs-second-moment duality and shows label noise is not required, only model-class residuals.

nodes.name: Multiple descents are possible
nodes.section: 1 What is double descent?
nodes.statement: Not every dataset/model pair exhibits exactly two descents; under different settings there can be one, three, or more descents (Nakkiran et al. 2020; Chen et al. 2021).

nodes.name: Implicit bias of gradient descent justifies the min-norm choice
nodes.section: 4 Mathematical Intuition from Ordinary Linear Regression
nodes.statement: The min-norm interpolation problem (ProbP459.2) is the optimization problem that gradient descent implicitly minimizes in the overparameterized regime (see Appendix on implicit bias).

nodes.name: 'Variance' terminology slightly abused without centering
nodes.section: 4 Mathematical Intuition from Ordinary Linear Regression
nodes.statement: Without centering $X$, $X^T X$ is the second-moment matrix rather than the empirical covariance, so the words 'vary' and 'variance' are used informally; the geometric intuition is unchanged.

nodes.name: Linear-regression intuition extends to NNGP-limit deep networks
nodes.section: 6 Intuition Extends to Nonlinear Models
nodes.statement: Infinite-width neural networks (e.g. the Neural Network Gaussian Process limit of Lee et al. 2017) reduce to linear regression on a particular feature map $F_\theta(X)$, so the three-factor analysis applies via the spectrum of $F_\theta(X)$.

nodes.name: Noise is not required; only model-class residuals are
nodes.section: 6 Intuition Extends to Nonlinear Models
nodes.statement: Random label noise is not necessary for double descent; what matters is the existence of residual errors $E$ from the perspective of the model class, which can be entirely deterministic (e.g. a nonlinear model trying to fit a noiseless linear relationship).
